Helen Morgan

Helen Morgan

London [helenmorgan@phonecoop.coop]

Helen Morgan  

If any theoretical body of work such as psychoanalysis is sealed off from other fields of study, it can become internally consistent but arid and lifeless. Because it is so hard to challenge a system of thought from the inside, it is imperative that we open our minds to the findings from other allied fields of study. Interesting things can happen when traditionally independent disciplines are placed alongside each other, and this book is a fine example of that approach. Jean Knox has done an impressive amount of work exploring, not only her own field of psychoanalytic thinking, but also those of other close disciplines, and she presents us with her findings, thoughts and conclusions from that study. This makes for a challenging read for, like any good book, it makes one think.

Knox argues convincingly that the findings from research in interpersonal neurobiology and developmental studies lead to the conclusion that it is from the infant's early relational experience with key attachment figures that a sense of self-agency, and of self, emerges.

I was, initially, somewhat disappointed as I began to read this book. I had imagined from the title and subtitle that it would address these topics in terms of specific instances. Instead the author takes the view, as she remarks at the end of the final chapter, that uncertainty and dilemma are implicit in the everyday work of the psychotherapist, and something to be continually struggled with. On further reading my disappointment was replaced by appreciation, and I found this book to be a careful, honest and deeply thoughtful account of the author's work with some of her more problematic patients over the years in private practice. She divides these in Part I into three chapters dealing with obsess ional disorders, problems of space, relying heavily on the work of Balint and his ‘philobats’ and ‘ocnophils’ (p. 16) and those patients who carry a sense of entitlement. Part II, which I found much the most interesting section of the book, is entitled ‘Love, Hate and the Erotic’. And Part III consists again of three chapters with the overall title of ‘Challenges to the Psychotherapeutic Frame’ and deals, firstly, with hysterical patients and the effect they may have on the therapist in terms of countertransference enactment, followed by a long account of a patient who was largely absent from her sessions. The final chapter does address individual examples of dilemmas she has encountered, but these, although doubtless significant in terms of transference/countertransference, are what I would call management issues: whether or not to fetch a glass of water for a thirsty patient, or remove a spider on the ceiling above a patient who is phobic about insects.

The three chapters in the middle section are written, as is most of the book, from the point of view of the author's subjectivity and present an account of a therapist constantly struggling to define and redefine those elements of her own humanity that her patients can most make use of.

In the first of these chapters, on ‘Love’, she starts by quoting a remark attributed to Ferenczi: ‘It is the physician's love that heals the patient’ (p. 51), and goes on to elaborate her hypothesis that, unless patients can sometimes arouse loving feelings in the therapist, a truly positive outcome is unlikely to be achieved. In attempting to specify what she means by loving feelings, she is careful to exclude those moments of satisfaction that may arise as a result of the patient's improvement as being merely a product of her own narcissism, but later goes on to enumerate those qualities in the patient which may arouse loving feelings in the therapist. I was a little confused as to the difference between these two positions but I think she is stressing the spontaneity of such feelings which may arise in many different scenarios, ‘paradoxically, … when a patient is finally able to vent his/her rage and hate towards me’ (p. 51). In the end she defines these feelings as moments of extreme tenderness based in the pre-oedipal, emotional and fondling relationship with the mother'.

Cathy Urwin 1949-2012

Barbie Antonis and Wendy Cartwright

Wendy Cartwright

[barbie.antonis@gmail.com]

[wendyjcartwright@gmail.com]

Wendy Cartwright  

At the time of her death Cathy Urwin was a Consultant Child and Adult Psychotherapist and Research Fellow at the Tavistock Clinic, which she had joined in 2004. She was lead researcher on the Tavistock's Babies-in-Groups Study, and a senior member of the Autism Service for Children and Families. She was making a major contribution, as a teacher and supervisor, on the Child Psychotherapy doctoral programme at the Tavistock, and as the external examiner on the Child Clinical Doctorate at the British Association of Psychotherapists/Birkbeck. She was also teaching on the Adult Training of the British Association of Psychotherapists. The BJP pays tribute to her life and work - Ed.

This is an appreciation rather than an obituary, an account of a friendship which is so bound up with our work that the two are inextricable. It is a shock to lose a friend unexpectedly, with the painful mourning of what is not to be. There is the loss of the potential, of work uncompleted, and the future plans for travel, painting and sharing Cathy's beloved Cornwall.

Cathy Urwin was the first friend I [BA] met and made in July 1974 when I arrived in Cambridge to take up a postgraduate research post in the Medical Applications of Psychology Unit at 5 Station Road (aka the ‘Unit’), headed by Dr Martin Richards. At that time she was at King's College, having embarked on her doctoral research on language development in blind babies. To my great good fortune it transpired that we actually lived around the corner from each other, so it was possible to get to know her in a personal way from then. Possible to discover her fun, her intellectual rigour, her curiosity about people and to see the strength she had when confronted by personal conflicts and pain. This beginning became a solid foundation for a deep friendship which endured till she died in June this year.

By the early 1980s, having worked in Nottingham and Oxford for a while, Cathy returned to Cambridge to take up post-doctoral research work within the Child Care and Development Unit (formerly ‘the Unit’) still led by Martin Richards. Whilst there she presented a series of seminars on Melanie Klein and it was there as a (mature) undergraduate that I [WC] first came across her. This was an introduction to Klein's work and it was spell-binding as her quiet and thoughtful delivery enabled us to begin to grasp a set of new and fascinating ideas. I retain to this day a sense of her pleasure in imparting these ideas to the seminar group, eyes alive, her attention focussed and ready for discussion. That quality remained until the very last weeks of her life.

Cathy had many talents and we have come to realize that we only knew aspects of her abilities that she generously shared with us. Cathy read and reviewed with us our proposal for a Child Clinical Doctorate with Birkbeck, University of London. It was a rewarding experience. After this informal exchange, she became a formal external assessor of the programme, during its validation by Birkbeck. With the Clinical Doctorate well in place, Cathy became the external examiner for the programme. Janine Sternberg  

It is hard to know when trying to write a review of less than 1500 words how to fit in all that I would want to say about this book - yet I think this dilemma reflects a problem that the editors had in creating their book. The book simply strains to contain within itself so much - at times it succeeds brilliantly, while at other times it left me dissatisfied, wishing for much more that I thought should have been included or elaborated on. There is enough material to fill at least two books. Even the physicality of the book exemplifies this: it is a couple of inches wider than most books to which we are accustomed, which, while looking very attractive, actually makes it harder to hold.

As with so many edited books it is probably not really intended to be read from beginning to end, but rather to be dipped into as the reader wishes. Nevertheless, unlike many edited volumes, it has a clear rationale in the way it is presented, being divided into four parts. Part I gives historical background; Part II, the most substantial part of the book, concentrates on developmental phases from infancy to adolescence, illustrating Anna Freud's approach to these through mainly clinical papers; Part III has papers on specialized work and Part IV has brief personal commentaries from those connected with the Anna Freud Centre. There is also a rather strange appendix giving biographical details of some of those mentioned in other chapters or who were connected with the Anna Freud Centre over the years, but which, inevitably, is very partial, thus not giving biographical details of some people who were much involved, or who were indeed mentioned, but whom we hear no more about. At times when there were lists of those who were involved in various study groups it felt rather like name checking, ensuring that no-one would feel left out - and yet of course many people were. It must have been hard for the editors to have had a realistic idea about who their readers may be. Did they anticipate that it would be those already familiar with Anna Freud and her ideas, or those possibly coming from a position of relative ignorance? Those who are deeply involved in the world of child psychotherapy and familiar with the type of detailed and careful case histories described in the clinical chapters or those for whom such stories would be a wonderful revelation? As someone familiar with reading those sort of case histories I enjoyed and appreciated the accounts of clinical work but found myself wanting more of the aspects I was unfamiliar with - for example, about Anna Freud's influence on education and legal matters.

Cognitive-Analytic Therapy in A Group: Reflections on A Dialogic Approach

Jason Hepple

Jason Hepple

56 Preston Road, Yeovil BA20 2BX [Jason.Hepple@sompar.nhs.uk]

Jason Hepple  

cognitive-analytic therapy (CAT), group psychotherapy, personality disorder, survivors of sexual abuse, dialogic psychotherapy

Cognitive-Analytic Therapy (CAT) (Ryle & Kerr, 2002) is a brief, integrative psychological therapy developed by Dr Anthony Ryle and others over the last 25 years. CAT is often used as an individual therapy for clients with personality disorder and is widespread within the NHs and private sectors in the UK and several countries abroad. CAT is being increasingly applied in group settings in the NHS. CAT, being at its heart a psychotherapy based on a relational understanding of human development, would seem to have much to offer in a group setting. This paper briefly reviews previous ways that the CAT model has been used in groups and then goes on to describe the author's experience of a one-year group carried out in South-West England. The therapeutic approach used adapts the CAT tools to a group setting, draws on CAT's dialogic underpinnings and shares some broader concepts with psychodynamic approaches.

Boarding School Syndrome

Simon Partridge

Simon Partridge

27 Beresford Road, London N2 8AT [simonpartridge846@btinternet.com]

Simon Partridge  

Dear Editor

It is good to see Elizabeth Standish continuing the debate on boarding school syndrome (BJP 28(2): 268), sparked off by Joy Schaverien (2011). I am however not convinced that she has been ‘misunderstood’. She says she has ‘no doubts about the detrimental effect of early parental deprivation’. But then why does she continue to make excuses for therapists who can't see this. Why does the responsibility rest with the patient or client to say how ‘awful’ it is? In my case I certainly gave clues that I hadn't been through a pleasant process, but I received the distinct impression that this was not germane to the psychoanalytic business. Then like a good boarding school boy I shut up.

As I raised in my original response (BJP 28(1): 129-31), there is a question about the efficacy of dyadic therapy as a modality for treating boarding school syndrome. This syndrome is the result of familial pressures reinforced by the practices and assumptions of boarding school and ultimately sanctioned by the wider culture of the upper-class elite. We are dealing here with the psychological consequences of the actions and assumptions of a series of interlocking groups in the face of which a child is virtually powerless. An individual therapist who can help a patient out of the emotional disablement engendered by such ‘relationships’ may leave the patient concerned with continuing problems vis-à-vis his/her family and the wider supporting culture. A psycho-emotional problem may have been resolved but the issue of how then to relate to the culture of origin can become deeply problematic and generate its own problems. It is in this context that ongoing group support can be beneficial - it certainly was for me. That is the view of current trauma experts like Judith Herman (2001), and Tal Astrachan, Carla Bernardes and Judith Herman (2010), when issues of power and isolation are so prevalent.

Simon Partridge

From the Editor

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[annscottbjp@aol.com]

Ann Scott  

I am pleased that correspondence about Martin Kemp's ‘Dehumanization, guilt and large group dynamics with reference to the West, Israel and the Palestinians’ continues in this issue of the BJP. My purpose here is to respond to the substantive questions about the editorial process for the article that were posed in the last issue by Mary Adams, Jane Polden, and James Astor (Letters, BJP 28(2): 264-267). Among other strands, three themes stand out from their letters: why was the article treated differently from other submissions, in being framed by an Editor's Note? What were the peer reviewers' assessments of the original article? Why the neutral tone of the published article, and why was it imposed on the author by the BJP? These are all valid questions, cogently argued, and I welcome the opportunity to respond.

To start with, the rationale for the Editor's Note. There was, in the first place, both the political sensitivity of the topic and the question ‘why a clinical journal?’ for publication of the article. In my view, these called for acknowledgement and commentary, in both online and print formats. In addition, I took the view that the publishing history of the article was significant in and of itself, in terms of process, and that it would be valuable, on scholarly grounds, to provide a brief account of this process.

Jane Polden suggests that the peer review process was used ‘for some other purpose than to address issues of academic quality and relevance’. I can reassure her, and readers who may have had the same thought, that the intention was precisely to address academic quality and relevance, from different perspectives on the situation in the Middle East. It is also true, as my Editor's Note indicated, that the political and psychic sensitivities of the topic led me to select peer reviewers who had their own experience of - and view of - the conflict. Not to have done so would have introduced bias. The phrase ‘constituences in the conflict’ was however not spelled out because to do so risked providing clues about the identity of the peer reviewers. Reflecting further, one could say that any peer reviewer of a journal submission represents a constituency, as each reviewer will normally speak from a particular psychoanalytic perspective. Dehumanization, Guilt and Large Group Dynamics with Reference to the West, Israel and the Palestinians

Mary Adams

Mary Adams

London [mary.adams@btinternet.com]

Mary Adams  

Dear Editor

Thank you to Martin Kemp for his thoughtful and important paper (BJP 27(4): 383-406) on ways that we can understand the traumas and dehumanization of Jews and Palestinians. Ongoing discussion of the profound and intergenerational psychological effects of such dehumanization is surely incumbent upon the psychoanalytic community when acts of genocide and discrimination continue in the world. One effect of trauma is to paralyse the ability to think, and in our psychoanalytic work our role is to aid the thinking process, help explore the processes of cause and effect, and facilitate the mourning that plays a critical role in breaking the cycle of repetition compulsion. If we cannot, as a psychoanalytic community, apply this approach in an open discussion of what is happening in Gaza, then there is something very wrong happening.

As Kemp points out, adopting a neutral position can in some situations become a turning a blind eye, blocking thinking and discussion. In this respect, it seems unfortunate that he was required by the BJP to seek ‘ever-more neutral words and phrasings’. It is as though we really do not have faith that our psychoanalytic thinking can lead to a fruitful intercourse and greater understanding.

Mary Adams

Editorial

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[annscottbjp@aol.com]

Ann Scott  

In the last year, the Editorial Board and I have been working on a revision of the Journal's Aims and Scope statement. It had been unchanged since the Journal was founded in the 1980s, and through a process of iteration we sought a form of wording that would replenish the Journal's vision, encompassing the many changes that have taken place in analytic psychotherapy in the last 25 years. The statement, which is now available on the BJP pages of the Wiley-Blackwell website, retains the Journal's original clinical focus on individual, group and institutional practice. At the same time, it places new emphasis on a dialogue between ‘private practice and institutionally based practice’, with its ‘differing potentials and constraints’, its different unconscious dynamics. We welcome theoretical papers and reflective research papers; acknowledge the changing regulatory context for our work; and reaffirm the Journal's traditional attention to professional, historical, cultural and political issues.

Many of these themes are reflected in this issue. We begin with Linda Buckingham's far-reaching theoretical reconsideration of projective identification. Arguing that confusions have accumulated in the uses and meanings of the term through the work of Bion and Ogden, she proposes ‘a return to Melanie Klein's original concept which focuses on the mental activity of the person in whose mind the projective identification takes place’. The paper is illustrated with vignettes from her practice as a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist.

Turning to the dynamic between individual and institutional practice, a variety of perspectives on individual work in the consulting room are represented. Anna Bravesmith, within a Jungian tradition and with a particular focus on the transcendent function, sensitively explores the ‘interplay between silence and speech’, recording and illustrating a number of types of silence: ‘defensive, hostile, entrenched … creative, enriching’. Angela King, from a relational perspective, presents a detailed case study of a 53 year-old client awaiting sex-reassignment surgery (male to female). King skilfully deploys both the language of countertransference (and its struggle) and the language of ‘personal transformation’ in terms of ‘an archetypal journey of life, death and rebirth’.

The Impact of Early Life Trauma on Health and Disease by Ruth Lanius, Eric Vermetten and Clare Pain. Published by Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 2010; 315 pages; £55.00; $95.00

Jean Knox

Jean Knox

[jm.knox@btinternet.com]

Jean Knox  

Reading this book was a rather humbling experience in that I realized that there is so much more research on the impact of early life trauma than I knew, even though I was familiar with quite a number of seminal papers in the field. One of the remarkable aspects of the book is the range of research that it covers, from the epidemiology of childhood trauma and the history of professional attitudes to the problem, through diagnostic controversies, psychosocial issues, longitudinal studies on the immediate and long-term neurobiological, psychological and physical effects of early relational trauma, to the implications all these hold for clinical work with children and adults who have suffered early-life trauma. This huge body of research is discussed and summarized in three sections, each of which has short co-authored chapters, so that the expertise of key researchers and clinicians across the whole field of traumatology is represented. The editors of the book are three psychiatrists, Ruth Lanius and Claire Pain from Canada, and Eric Vermetten from the Netherlands, all neuroscience and trauma research specialists who also explore the implications of empirical research for clinical psychotherapy practice.

The focus of almost all these papers is on the hugely damaging impact that neglect or abuse by primary caregivers has on the psychological and emotional development of the human infant, creating life-long consequences in terms of brain development, attachment and affect dysregulation, altered stress responses and a range of psychological symptoms, from the flashbacks and hyper-arousal of PTSD to altered perception, epileptic-type phenomena and dissociative states of varying degrees of severity, including borderline personality and dissociative identity disorder. This evidence from neurobiology powerfully supports the argument that it is real-life experience rather than innate unconscious phantasy that determines most of the problems our patients bring to the consulting room and so is highly relevant to our clinical practice.

Michael Rustin

London [m.j.rustin@uel.ac.uk]

Michael Rustin  

This is an unusual and ingenious publication. Printed on white card, it folds out into a ten-page wall chart, each page (10 cm2) corresponding to a decade in the history of psychoanalysis. The reverse side contains first an introduction and a key to the timeline which sets out the authors' approach and then seven pages of narrative history, set out by decade, amplifying the information contained on the chart. The chart uses a colour code to identify the different theoretical tendencies, and their main geographical locations, through which the 20th century development of the field is set out. Each tendency is represented by the principal publications associated with it, and by psychoanalytic events, such as the foundation of leading clinics and institutes. The colour-coded tendencies and locations are Jung and Jungians (Existential Psychoanalysts, mostly Swiss; British; [after 1926] Kleinians and [after 1950] Independents; French; Lacan and Lacanians; non-Lacanians; Freud and Freudians [after 1938], mostly in England and America; Adler; Rank; Social and Cultural Theorists; the Budapest School; [after 1945] Interpersonalism, Relationalism. In the middle of the chart, fully appropriately, lies Freud himself, with The Interpretation of Dreams cited as the inaugural work. It is suggested that vertical movement down the chart roughly signifies differences between more intrapsychic and more environmentalist approaches, with the middle part of chart, where Freud and the Freudians are located interpreted as a synthesis of the two. International Psychoanalytic Congresses and Presidents, and major world events, are set out chronologically at the base of the chart. Not a centimetre has been wasted.

The authors have succeeded in presenting a great deal of information in a legible way, and in a way which is pleasing to the eye. This represents a considerable achievement of graphic design, as well as of concise selection, summary and synthesis of psychoanalytic work over its full range. As this publication measures only 2 metres by 20 centimetres (or 40 centimetres if the reverse side is placed beneath the chart), it is well adapted for a classroom or library wall.

My review copy of Playing with Dynamite arrived in timely fashion in the week following the then Justice Minister, Kenneth Clarke's ill-advised remarks about rape sentencing in a radio interview. Clarke proposed halving sentences for those entering guilty pleas early in the court process, thereby, in his view, sparing additional trauma to victims and costs to the criminal justice system. This proposed policy was challenged by rape victims, and the ensuing public outcry reflected the continuing conflict in the public mind between its capacity for humanity and understanding and its demand for justice and revenge (The Guardian, 2011).

In recent years there have been more high profile cases involving women as perpetrators of violence; ‘Baby P’, a 17 month-old boy, died in 2007 in the London Borough of Haringey following a history of injuries and abuse by those caring for him. His mother, Tracey Connelly, was deemed, according to the tabloids, ‘a sex-obsessed slob’ and was convicted of actions contributing to the death of her infant son. Vanessa George, a nursery worker deemed first ‘an angel’, ‘a second mother’ until convicted with Angela Allen of multiple sexual assaults on babies and children in her care, when she became ‘an evil monster’. The Head of the Crown Prosecution Service stated that: ‘No one who heard what was said in court can begin to understand why these two women committed such shocking acts of child abuse’. She commented that: ‘They acted in a way that ordinary people will find impossible to understand’ (CPS, 2009).

Editorial

Ann Scot

Ann Scot

[annscottbjp@aol.com]

Ann Scot  

Questions of a natural propensity to altruism in human beings; of the preservation of ‘embryonic self-states’ in patients and of ‘endurance’ in the clinician; and of different forms of guilt are addressed in the first three, searching papers in this issue of the Journal. We continue with a group of wide-ranging papers on the theme of ‘Psychoanalysis and Ethics’. Aspects of the clinical cultures of Australia, the United States and the UK are represented within the section.

In a development of an earlier paper published in the BJP (Music, 2009), Graham Music argues that psychoanalytic thinking ‘might have underestimated the role of altruism as a natural feature of human development’, and that we need to ‘re-establish the fact that being kind and caring is also part of human nature, and also has a place in psychoanalytic psychotherapy’. Recognizing that Freud's view was, broadly, that human beings are ‘naturally self-interested, drive-driven, destructive and aggressive’, Music uses findings from neuroscience, attachment and developmental research on the capacity for empathy and altruism, in a most nuanced way, to argue this different position. Two vignettes from work with patients whose very difficult backgrounds had inclined them to brittle, unfeeling negativity illustrate the type of change that may become possible when this shift of conceptual perspective is held in mind.

The late Nina Farhi believed that the level of disturbance in her patients - individuals ‘who had survived near impossible emotional and psychological circumstances’ - could not be treated or theorized ‘within the psychoanalytic orthodoxy of her time’. Jean White authoritatively locates the evolution of Farhi's clinical thought, with its ‘continual emphasis on unconscious resourcefulness in the service of psychic survival’, in the tradition of Marion Milner and Winnicott, but with its own, particular development in the area of intersubjectivity. White scrupulously assesses Farhi's three major papers (one published posthumously), including in her discussion the ensuing, published commentary by colleagues. She also suggests that there may be a risk of a merged or fusional state, in Farhi's conceptualization of the intersubjective, all the time recognizing the creative depth in Farhi's work.

Finding the Possible in the Impossible: The Clinical and Theoretical Work of Nina Farhi

Jean White

Jean White

Flat 5, 77 Sunnyside Road, London N19 3SL. [jeanwhite333@hotmail.com]

Jean White  

psychoanalytic endurance, philosophical romanticism, Winnicott, Milner, unconscious resourcefulness in the service of psychic survival, annealing identification

In a psychoanalytic career spanning three decades, Nina Farhi (1943-2009) worked primarily with people who had survived near impossible emotional and psychological circumstances. In a series of clinical papers, she theorized the ways in which her patients had managed to preserve embryonic self-states against all odds and the arduous, imaginative and resourceful psychoanalytic work required to transform these vestiges of survival into creative living. This paper traces the evolution of Farhi's clinical thought, from her surprising and fresh uses of particular concepts of Winnicott's to her original re-working of some of Marion Milner's foundational insights. It explores the ways in which Farhi's clinical practice was original and the clinical and theoretical legacy she leaves.

Editorial Introduction

Caroline Hallett and Elizabeth O'Loughlin

Elizabeth O'Loughlin

[carolinehlltt@gmail.com]

[elizaariadne@blueyonder.co.uk]

Elizabeth O'Loughlin  

In this group of invited papers the BJP raises the question of the ethics underpinning psychoanalysis. In 1925, aware of the unfinished nature of his work, Freud wrote:

Finally, I am no longer alone, an eager crowd of fellow-workers is ready to make use of what is unfinished or doubtful, and I can leave to them that part of the work that I should otherwise have done myself. (Freud, 1925, p. 249)

Since then the psychoanalytic field has diversified in ways Freud could hardly have imagined, with the evolution of theory and practice in both private and public sector contexts. The theme of Ethics may call to mind organizational frameworks for practice, addressing such important issues as confidentiality and boundaries. In this issue we take a more general view of ethics in the spirit of encouraging breadth and diversity, with the inclusion of papers from Australia, USA and the UK. We present four papers concerned with the nature of psychoanalytic work showing how orientation and context influence the ethical stance of the psychoanalytic practitioner. We hope that readers will identify with some of these ideas, and will be challenged by others, to reflect on how we work and whether there are ethics particular to psychoanalysis beyond technique and moral considerations in the individual case.

Michael Plastow describes the discourse of ‘retail therapy’ and its conflict with that of psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Susan Schwartz presents an account of a practice whose ethic pushes against the demands of society for ‘well-being’ and ‘happiness’. Glen O. Gabbard and Gabrielle S. Hobday show how medical practitioners who have acted unethically may be worked with analytically. Caroline Hallett presents the conflict between the demands of the institution and the ethics of treatment.

We open the section with a paper from Australian analyst Michael Plastow, ‘Retail Therapy: The Enjoyment of the Consumer’, in which he presents his view of shopping's inadequacy as a response to psychic suffering. In this thought-provoking consideration of societal trends the Lacanian concepts of desire, castration and loss are placed at the centre of the human subject. By highlighting the contemporary discourse of rights versus responsibilities, Plastow proposes that excessive consumption acts as a regressive influence on the psyche, entrapping us in polymorphous perversity and keeping us from a more mature relationship to our own desire.

Boarding School Syndrome

Elizabeth Standish

Elizabeth Standish

[liz.standish@btinternet.com]

Elizabeth Standish  

Dear Editor

I had mixed reactions on reading the letters by Nick Duffell and Simon Partridge (BJP 28(1): 126-31). One was delight at having provoked two such lively responses, followed quickly by feeling misunderstood. Perhaps I need to clarify that I have no doubts about the detrimental effect of early parental deprivation whether through the death of a parent, being brought up in the ‘Care’ system, being sent away to boarding school or however it occurs. And I do recognize that there is a particular problem for those in the latter category in that they are often told they are privileged, and thought to be so. But both writers seem to assume that I am likely to be impressed by ‘well-spoken schoolboys’ or that I do not recognize the ‘emotional illiteracy’ of many upper-class British families.

My intent in writing my original letter was to try to understand the problems in relation to ‘boarding school syndrome’ experienced by a number of patients in therapy. In so doing a number of ideas have been attributed to me which I do not recognize, and I have stirred up some angry responses. It is clear that Partridge and many others also felt misunderstood by their therapists/analysts, and feel angry with them.

I don't deny that professional incompetence exists, or that psychoanalytic thinking has to move on. But might there be something else that is being misunderstood? Partridge refers to the ‘distanced couch’. I am not sure whether the ‘deficit’ he refers to is that which he experienced in his analysis or the much earlier deficit in his childhood or both. But if it is the latter, this seems to me to touch on the rather large topic of what can and cannot happen in therapy or analysis. As Duffell says, it is important that therapists do not ‘ignore how the past impacts the present’ and that we address the difficulties patients experience in current relationships both within and outside the consulting room. What we cannot do is put right that early deficit, a concept which may be understood at a rational level, but which can so readily give rise to the feeling that the earlier deprivation is being repeated - ‘you don't understand what I really want from you’. The hope is that, through learning to relate differently, in a more trusting way, to the therapist, something changes.

Jennifer Silverstone

Jennifer Silverstone

London [J.Silverstone@btconnect.com]

Jennifer Silverstone  

Here it is, sixteen years after her death, a book in the new History of Psychoanalysis Series, an eagerly anticipated book on the life and work of Dr Nina Coltart. It is constructed as a ‘garland’, a collection of pieces around and about Nina Coltart - a book of reminiscences, essays and some previously unpublished material. This ‘garland’ of a book invites many, and varied people, from family, friends, analysands and supervisees to think about, review and comment on the life of Nina Coltart. Everything is here included, her book reviews, letters, two obituaries she wrote, a specimen of her calligraphy, her curriculum vitae: stuff that a woman in her position would have been, and was, asked to produce in her 69 years of life.

This motley collection is divided up into two sections, Part I: Tributes and Part II: Uncollected Writings. Each of these sections is split into subsections and the book has 51 chapter headings. Despite the long list of contents the book is hard to navigate and the provenance of the papers is not always clear. For example, when looking up Brendan MacCarthy, whose piece is printed as Chapter 17, one does not expect to read a previously published piece from an obituary he wrote in the British Psychoanalytical Society Bulletin. This is a posthumous reprint, and the reference to his surviving wife, children and grandchildren seems unnecessary and sets the tone for the curious lack of boundaries to come.

Nina Coltart was a distinguished psychoanalyst. The seminal events in her personal history, of which she made no secret, are therefore in the public domain. Having studied languages at Oxford she went on to study medicine, and after having qualified she began her analytic training. She garnered, among other titles, Director of the London Clinic of Psychoanalysis. She had a fine reputation as a clinician, a diagnostician and, later in her career, a writer. She was also thought of as a maverick and sometimes lone voice in the psychoanalytic community, in part for freely moving without prejudice from the Institute of Psychoanalysis to Arbours to Squiggle and to Nafisayat, and I am sure to many others. She also taught and supported psychoanalytic trainings outside London, and she offered the organizations with which she became involved succour, advice, support and guidance. She had the ability to move without prejudice in and out of the conservative tradition that still defines psychoanalysis. She referred those whom she diagnosed to a wide range of therapists, always with the patients' best interests at heart, which too made her exceptional. A referral from Nina Coltart almost always ‘took’. If you were invited to treat someone she had seen that day, invariably the prospective patient would be on the phone within the hour.

Why Things Matter: The Place of Values in Science, Psychoanalysis and Religion by David M. Black. Published by Routledge, Hove, 2011; 216 pages; £60.00 hardback, £22.99 paperback

Kenneth Wright

Kenneth Wright

London [kjt.wright@doctors.org.uk]

Kenneth Wright  

At least until the middle of the 19th century, religion, underpinned by the Church, was the sacrosanct repository of human values. These values were ordained by God, the creator of all things, and although Man often failed to live up to them, this in no way threatened their integrity. By the end of the 19th century, this situation had changed dramatically, and by the end of the 20th a radically different world-view had taken shape. The planet we inhabit and Man himself are now explained by the natural sciences and what originally was a provocative and no doubt blasphemous remark of Nietzsche that God is dead is to all intents and purposes a defining feature of our time. The religious domain no longer provides an anchor for moral values and this has made for a world of confusing freedoms and a kind of moral void.

This is the cultural starting-point for David Black's interesting book which begins with two searching questions. Firstly, if there is no longer a divine underpinning of human values, how could it ever be claimed that one value should be followed rather than another? And secondly, if there is no longer a religious container for such values (a setting in which they can be contemplated and talked about), how could they ever maintain a sufficient presence in our lives to exert a guiding force?

Black's argument is broadly as follows. As the new scientific world-view based on empirical study and logical argument gained ground, the older scholastic (religious) view of Man as having a divine soul and a consciousness of good and evil was gradually eclipsed. In the world-view of natural science, Man was increasingly seen as just another part of the material world and any serious concern with non-material things such as consciousness, subjectivity and values was redundant.

The absence of values in this way of thinking is a major focus of Black's concern and he illustrates the potential consequences of such value-free science in a vignette at the beginning of the first chapter.

Ann Scott

Ann Scott  

The BJP is delighted to be publishing a three-part series of articles on the innovative psychoanalytic work of Armando B. Ferrari, in this and the next two issues of the Journal. Ferrari's work had a special focus on the body, ‘not only as mind's first object, but … the object out of which mind originates’. Our series, which has been in development over the last three years, comprises two translations from work published in Italian in 2006, and a substantial introduction to Ferrari's thought by Richard Carvalho. Dr Carvalho has translated the article by Paulo Carignani which appears in this issue, and that by Fausta Romano, which will appear in print in February 2013. (All three pieces are published together on Early View this summer; Carvalho's introduction appears in print in November this year.) The three articles, taken together, allow readers to consider the implications for clinical practice of Ferrari's view, in Carignani's words, that: ‘The body is the source of the mind, that for which mind is responsible and to which it is answerable. It is not, of course, the body in an anatomical, medical sense, but the body as it is lived, which is dynamic and in constant transformation: the body which emanates emotions and sensations and by which, in turn, it itself is constantly changed.’ The BJP is very grateful to Richard Carvalho for his commitment to the project and his sensitive industry, as both translator and author; to Teresa Drew, our copy-editor and proofreader, who has worked with meticulous care to prepare the three articles for publication; and to Janine Sternberg and Hazel Robinson for their initial facilitation of the project.

Contrasting methodologies inform the articles presented in ‘Public Sector Practice’. Rosemary Rizq considers the organizational dynamics of the UK National Health Service's Improving Access to Psychological Therapies programme, in ‘The ghost in the machine: IAPT and organizational melancholia’. Drawing on a rich seam of analytic and group-relations theory, from Freud's ‘Mourning and melancholia’ to more recent Kleinian and post-Kleinian work on anxieties and defences in work settings, Rizq explores the ‘tendency for IAPT services to systematically disavow feelings of loss and vulnerability in both staff and patients’. The article importantly complements and develops Rizq's earlier work on anxiety and envy in the IAPT programme (Rizq, 2011).

The Training Value of the Psychodynamic Psychotherapy Long Case: A Psychiatry Trainee's Perspective

Jonathan Green

Jonathan Green

Yorkshire Regional Secure Unit, Newton Lodge, Ouchthorpe Lane, Wakefield WF1 3SP. [jonathangreen@nhs.net]

Jonathan Green  

psychiatric training, psychotherapy long case, doctor-patient relationship, transference, countertransference

In order to fully satisfy eligibility criteria for membership of the Royal College of Psychiatrists, trainees must demonstrate satisfactory attainment of competencies in psychotherapy. Evidence required includes a Psychotherapy ‘ACE’ (assessment of clinical expertise) and completion of two psychotherapy cases in two modalities.

With training posts in the Yorkshire deanery becoming European Working Time Directive compliant, a trainee gains less experience in their actual clinical post. Therefore, what benefit could a trainee derive from further time away from their posts in order to gain experience in a subspecialty that very few of us will pursue long-term? I have conducted a 40-week period of psychodynamic psychotherapy. I also received weekly supervision sessions with an experienced therapist. I will reflect on my positive experiences completing a psychodynamic long case and describe how the skills I have developed are transferable to most aspects of practice.

The role of the psychiatrist within the NHS is continually being redefined. The Department of Health's New Ways of Working initiative may result in fleeting patient contact, which may not be conducive to in-depth psychodynamic work. I would suggest that, at this uncertain time, psychiatrists might wish to push for further involvement with psychotherapy. The first step in this process is to ensure that all psychiatric trainees are adequately trained in psychotherapy. Efforts should be made to ensure that, as working hours become more unpredictable, psychiatric trainees are afforded protected time slots in order to complete psychotherapy training.

This issue of the Journal continues the exploration of the work of Armando B. Ferrari. We open with Richard Carvalho's masterly overview of Ferrari's work, following Paolo Carignani's consideration of ‘the body in psychoanalysis’ in the previous issue. Carvalho suggests that Ferrari's approach, which postulates a ‘direct relationship between body and mind’ that is in contrast to the object relations model ‘in which this relationship is mediated through the breast’, offers ‘an important avenue of approach’ to the treatment of psychosis, psychosomatic illness and anorexia. This last provides a link with the paper on anorexia and bulimia by Fausta Romano which is presented in the next issue of the Journal, and which will conclude our series. Laying out Ferrari's terminology (Concrete Original Object, vertical axis, horizontal axis, as denoting specific relationships between body, mind, and external world) Carvalho compares Ferrari's conceptual framework with Bion's. He goes on to show how the subject's ‘direct’ rather than mediated apperception of the ‘sensational and emotional life of his body’ has implications for the centrality of transference interpretation, without in any way dispensing with the idea of transference as ubiquitous; he develops this position with a rich illustration from his own clinical work.

Clinicians with a psychosocial perspective have had a longstanding interest in the relationship between culture and eating disorders in women, perhaps young women in particular. Yael A. Kadish rightly recognizes the importance of engagement with this debate, and carefully integrates a body of literature coming from feminist scholars and commentators, and critical social theorists, on the one hand, with John Steiner's work on pathological organizations and psychic retreats, on the other. She develops her argument with new conceptual terms that are intended to situate psychic experience within a framework of imposed norms, a ‘taxonomy of social desirability’. Using case material from two patients in their thirties with different eating disorders, she sensitively explores the way in which the ‘cultural imperative espousing the normalized body order’ manifests intrapsychically, differentiating between the clinical impact of early and later trauma.

The collection, Infant Observation and Research: Emotional Processes in Everyday Lives, that Cathy and I worked on editing together was published just as she was faced with the diagnosis of cancer (Urwin & Sternberg, 2012). She had felt unwell for the previous few months, but in the time leading up to that I had never heard her complain of anything. Rather she had shouldered all the burdens of editing a book in an enthusiastic and deeply committed way. She was able to see a copy of the book while very weak and knowing she was dying. She declared it ‘rather good’: this remains a source of great pleasure to me.

The book in some way represents the coming together of many of Cathy's professional interests. Cathy had worked for many years as an academic social scientist before training to be a child and adolescent psychotherapist; making links between her past and current working lives enabled her to see the ways in which the practice of infant observation - what we came to call the infant observation methodology - could be used in social science research. Cathy had been involved in a major project in Tower Hamlets in which infant observation was used alongside other methodologies, such as interviewing. In thinking about a wider use of infant observation as a research methodology, we emphasized the value of generalizing from the particular, seeing the impact of the experience on the observer/researcher as an important source of data.

This emphasis was foregrounded again in the ‘Babies-in-Groups Project’ that Cathy carried out with two other researchers, Ben Bradley and Jane Selby. This was within a laboratory setting, but influenced by naturalistic infant observation.

Liza Catan  

For 25 years the New Library of Psychoanalysis has disseminated bold and innovative advances in recent analytic thinking, both within and beyond the profession, and a new publication on what is arguably the keystone Kleinian concept, edited and introduced by two eminent London Kleinians, is a significant event. However, while both seasoned and novice readers will find many details of interest, my overall impression was of a divided and insufficiently

542

organized volume which suffers from a lack of clarity about its overall purpose and lacks a unifying argument.

The book falls into three sections, the first concentrating on the evolution of the concept of projective identification in Melanie Klein's clinical and theoretical understanding; the second covers near-to-source developments of the concept in the work of prominent London-based Kleinians; the third, and longest, section charts its wider dissemination and use in non-Kleinian strands of the British Psychoanalytic Society, other Western European countries (Germany, France, Italy and Spain), the United States and South America (Argentina, Brazil and Chile).

The opening chapter consists of an account by Elizabeth Spillius of her archival research into the evolution of Klein's thinking about projective identification. Presented in the form of brief notes with main themes and concepts presented in bold and reiterated in ever more summarized forms, this chapter feels like a pared-down précis of well digested ideas rather than (as I had hoped) conceptual exploration based on her original research. Spillius's chapter is followed first, by a reprinting of the 1952 version of Some Notes on Schizoid Mechanisms, then by several well-known, much-published papers on projective identification by prominent post-Kleinian thinkers - Bion, Rosenfeld, Joseph, Feldman and Sodré. These classics of post-Kleinian thinking are also introduced by Spillius, summarizing, under the authors' names - again picked out in bold - selected aspects of their papers, which are presented as facts about the papers rather than as analysis or evaluation. At this point, it was with a sense of having my thoughts directed, shaped and corralled, of having my freedom as a reader impinged upon, that the questions about intended readership began to find their answer: The Fate of a Concept is, at least in its early chapters, an academic ‘reader’ - a standard textbook, such as might service a university-based masters course. A sense of the intended readership began to form in my mind: the hard-pressed university tutor who would appreciate a volume which prescribed readings and main messages providing, in effect, a ready-made course ‘spec’, or the student grappling with deadline-dominated coursework. This was not what this reviewer had anticipated, perhaps, but a clear purpose nonetheless. However, following these papers on the early evolution of projective identification, the book changes its course; it ceases to be a higher education course ‘reader’ and becomes an exercise in the history of ideas, charting the evolution of the concept and its dissemination in a globalizing world. The Fate of a Concept, it transpires, is not one, but two books united - not entirely comfortably - within the same cover.

Angela King

Heath House, 156a Sandridge Road, St Albans AL1 4AP. [angela@insightful.me.uk]

Angela King  

adult psychotherapy, countertransference, gender, object relations, relational psychoanalysis, sexuality, transsexualism, unconscious

The importance of developing a certain consciousness in which one is present and autonomous while being intimately interconnected with larger meaning is an important dimension of a relational approach to psychotherapy. Based on the premise that both client and therapist bring something of themselves and of their respective past emotional experience to the therapeutic relationship, a relational approach to therapy is very attentive to the dynamics in the therapy room. It stresses the co-creation of the therapeutic relationship at conscious, explicit verbal levels and unconscious, implicit levels of functioning, and establishes the therapist's emotional behaviour as a significant factor in fostering change (Aron, 1996).

Therapist responsiveness to client's affective impact is discussed with emphasis on its centrality to clinical practice and its relationship to countertransference. A case study of the psychotherapeutic journey with ‘Dawn’ (previously ‘David’), a 53 year-old client who was awaiting sex-reassignment surgery, is presented which illustrates how the therapist's struggle in the countertransference represents part of a complex relational body/mind system of parallel processes, re-enactment and potential for therapeutic change.

8 Cornwall Grove, London W4 2LB [alejandro.reyes853@googlemail.com]

Alejandro Reyes  

Psychoanalysis, the Jewish science of Nazi lore, has traditionally had an awkward, uncomfortable relation with racism and other burning social problems. Freud, a characteristic secular, atheistic, European intellectual was himself a bit detached from his feelings on these issues but did not want psychoanalysis to become a Weltanschaung. In 1938, when asked to comment on the rise of European anti-Semitism he was reluctant to do so. Yet on that same occasion he did cast a sceptical view on the motivations of anti-racists both Christian and secular for harbouring a deeply buried racist and patronizing stance towards Jews deeply in their liberal humanistic considerations. For Fakhry Davids it was a lack of hard clinical evidence as to how racism works in the mind plus possibly the experience of his own angry counter transference to the possible causes of Freud's silence, which has pervaded psychoanalysis itself.

This book is underpinned by the author's personal experience of racism, first under the apartheid of his native South Africa, then as a brown/black foreigner in England. So, to his clinical skills and profound emotional experience we add an important element of political awareness to this book. His account of the two ‘banal’ racial incidents and of his own subjectivity undergoing a racist attack are enthralling and leave us in no doubt about the importance to know our own racism before attempting to know it in someone else's internal world.

For a long time racism has been left to the so called applied psychoanalysis. Clinical psychoanalysis applications have tended in the past to reduce racism into existing psychoanalytical models (e.g. Oedipal) or known psychological categories, and/or have relied on essentialist ideas exacerbating the polarity between the individual psyche and the social space. One of the many merits of this work is that it brings into the present the unjustly forgotten figures who are Davids's predecessors in his task like Joel Kovel, the heroic psychoanalyst from New York, or Frantz Fanon, the revolutionary psychiatrist and psychoanalyst to whom the author dedicates an entire, fascinating chapter. Although there is a great deal in this book that is valuable and thought provoking, like for example the chapters on group work, institutional racism and anti-Semitism, I have chosen to address the clinical and theoretical core of the author's work which is his original and more important contribution.

679 Rathdowne St., Carlton North, Victoria 3054, Australia. [plastow@internode.on.net]

Michael Plastow  

retail therapy, economics, consumer, perversion, psychoanalysis

The discourse of economics and consumerism has not only penetrated into the clinical setting; it has had a pervasive effect upon each of us and upon the society in which we live. This state of affairs is taken up by reference to the now commonly used phrase ‘retail therapy’, in order to examine the implications of the promotion of this concept. These ideas are further elaborated through an examination of the consumerist bent our societies have taken, promoting as they do an unfettered enjoyment of consumer goods. But for society to function and for desire to take root in the subject, it is proposed that there is a necessary loss of enjoyment which from psychoanalysis we can designate as castration. The contemporary difficulty to undergo such a loss is tied here to a prolongation of the state Freud described as polymorphously perverse. It is here that the psychoanalyst has an ethical responsibility to unveil whatever discourses function to alienate the subject from his or her desire.

Drawing upon Professor Higgins in George Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion as a template, and making use of clinical material, I will reflect upon the painful, poignant and self-inflicted inner loneliness of the narcissistic individual. In order to master early trauma, the narcissistic person constructs an outwardly substantial self in which he seeks to control others and the way he is perceived by others. In so doing he renounces the more emotionally vulnerable parts of himself, the very parts he needs in order to develop a more authentic self and emotionally connect with others. Sometimes a crack appears in his defensive narcissistic structure with the possibility of something more life-enhancing emerging.

I agreed with many of Martin Kemp's interesting thoughts and I appreciated his careful research, the breadth of his investigation, his judicious language and his courage in publishing this paper in a context where ‘the potential for giving offence’ can ‘take priority’ over a private discussion ‘weighted towards understanding’ (BJP 27(4): 383-406).

I wondered whether we can import this kind of analytic thinking into a situation like this where fanaticism is still dominant.

Alan Eppel  

Dear Editor

The letters in response to Martin Kemp's article ‘Dehumanization, Guilt and Large Group Dynamics’ (BJP 27(4): 383-406) confirm and repeat the deficiencies of his analysis. His article is academically lopsided with selective opinions and references that render it more polemical than scholarly. This is regrettable as an opportunity was lost to bring a fresh intellectual field of view to this problem.

Kemp completely omits the psychological impact on Israeli Jews of their total exclusion and dehumanization by the majority of the Arab world. It is the Israelis who are, in fact, subject to an apartheid exclusion by their neighbours in Syria, Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, etc.

It is not that Israelis lack empathy and compassion towards the Palestinians. The quotations from Israeli authorities that Kemp cites in the article, confirm the agonizing debates that occur in Israel about the destructive effects that persisting Israeli rule of a large Palestinian population has on both Palestinian and Israeli national identity and consciousness.

As Golda Meir said: ‘We can forgive the Arabs for killing our children, but we cannot forgive them for forcing us to kill their children. We will have peace with the Arabs when they love their children more than they hate us.’

What is completely missing from Kemp's analysis as a British psychotherapist is the unconscious conflict within the British psyche that leads to the projection of such hatred by so many in the British media and academia towards Israel. The British after all have ultimate responsibility for the Israel-Palestine conflict, and it is the British who may harbour unconscious guilt about this. The same unconscious guilt stems from the long history of British colonialism with its grievous manifestations in India and Ireland, just to name two other examples.

It is this guilt that is unconsciously projected onto the Jewish Israeli populace. As psychotherapists we must be mindful of the countertransference.

Alan B. Eppel

Lennox Thomas  

This important book nudges the barriers of theory and practice. Of these the most important is the drawing together of several important themes in psychoanalysis and charting a renaissance in classical theory. What is particular is that the clinical material is largely based around a patient group descended from enslaved people from the Caribbean, who migrated to the United Kingdom three or so generations ago. The tools for working with this population are presented and consider a range of traditional therapeutic principles as well as new ones. The book introduces the important issues of separation and attachment, setting out the effects over several generations. We are reminded of the experience of generational transmission of trauma and loss and the way that we might be shown this by our patients' behaviour. Many of the clinical examples illustrate difficulties that patients have both in parent/child relationships as well as in loving couple relationships. Fletchman Smith refers to this as coupling, the coming together of women and men which was made especially difficult because of the rules on the plantation. She talks particularly about the mothering of black men and women and in turn the mothering of their own children and how the experience of slavery had a detrimental effect on this most intimate of relationships. She sees this as the beginning of the devaluing and rupturing of mothering and the important bonding with the infant which continued in post-slavery society. This usually privileged relationship was sacrificed for the master's need for women to toil in the fields. Bonding with babies and partners was forbidden; the enslaved did not own their bodies, affections or romantic desires. Loving connections between the enslaved was kept secret so that children would not know their fathers. The slaves learned that open relationships led to exploitation and manipulation by plantation managers, the whipping or selling of a loved one as punishment for a troublesome man or woman.

Anna Bravesmith

Anna Bravesmith

59 Holmesdale Road, Highgate, London N6 5TH. [anna@jar59.fsnet.co.uk] [http://www.annabravesmithpsychotherapy.co.uk/]

Anna Bravesmith  

silence, dialogue, transcendent function, coniunctio, opposites, Jungian theory, language

In this paper the interplay between silence and the spoken words used by analyst and patient will be explored within the context of clinical practice. Both analyst and patient, it is argued, are engaged in a personal struggle to try to discover an integrative connection between silence, often experienced as nothingness, and speech, often experienced as suffocating or mendacious. The uses of silence in aiding speech to attain integrity will be described with reference to two clinical vignettes. Selections from psychoanalytic theory and practice will be discussed, throwing some light on silence and analytic spoken dialogue, and it will be argued that a Jungian perspective contributes a further, unique, insight through the concept of transcendent function. This is a way of seeing silence and speech as opposites, out of which new levels of meaning arise as a result of union and unconscious cooperation in the relationship between them. This union is known as coniunctio.

Elisabeth Young-Bruehl 1946-2011

Peter Wilson

Peter Wilson

London [peterjbwilson@btinternet.com]

Peter Wilson  

There is a rare group of speakers who can hold the attention of their audience so powerfully that no one wants the lecture to stop. Elisabeth Young-Bruehl was one of those exceptional people. She was a warm and compassionate woman whose sharp intelligence and lively curiosity never ceased to fascinate. Her knowledge was extensive, drawing as it did on a wide range of interests and on her unwavering passions for the human rights of people to pursue unfettered whatever form of creativity they sought. She began in academic philosophy and then moved more and more into politics and into psychoanalysis. The combination of all three interests and capabilities produced a remarkably gifted and versatile human being.

Her recent and sudden death at the age of 65 came as a major shock to all who knew her. Only last November, a mere month before she died, we had the privilege of listening to her at an Anna Freud Colloquium talking about her new work on Winnicott and her views on his relationship with Anna Freud. We were enthralled and some of us in the British Association of Psychotherapists hurried to invite her to speak again in the spring, an invitation she readily accepted.

It is no surprise that, in extending her skills to biography, she should have chosen Hannah Arendt in 1982 and Anna Freud in 1988 as her subjects. Both were women of considerable stature in their respective fields - Hannah Arendt in political theory, Anna Freud in child psychoanalysis. Both were Jewish refugees who had suffered and fled from the abominations of the Nazi regime. The nature of the human condition, the life of the mind and the plight of the vulnerable became matters of deep concern to both. And, in the pursuit of these interests, they brought formidable intellect and determination.

Both biographies received high acclaim, applauded for their exemplary mastery of both the facts and the cultures of the two women's lives. It is tribute to Young-Bruehl that they so entrusted her to permit entry into the experiences which they had undergone. She once said of the capacity for empathy (which showed so well in her writings) that it arose not so much from putting oneself into the place of the other as of allowing the other to establish a place in oneself.

This book is a collection of conference papers given at the second International Psychoanalytic Conference to take place in Belfast, and was sponsored by The Royal College of Psychiatrists, The Centre for Psychotherapy, The Belfast Trust, Northern Ireland Association for the Study of Psychoanalysis, The Northern Ireland Institute of Human Relations and the British Psychoanalytic Society.

The papers are printed in full plus the discussions that followed. Together they offer the reader a stimulating read. My one gripe with the book is that it appears incompletely edited. It is reasonable to put the conference within the context of the ash cloud that descended on Britain in 2010 but one reference would surely be enough. Likewise in the discussions that follow the papers, we could have been saved the repetitious introductions, the questions that are not answered, as well as the comments that sail away into the stratosphere as they sometimes do in such sessions.

However, the book offers a welcome collection of papers that link the subjects of aggression and violence and the development of these aspects of the human character. The quality of the papers, delivered by clinicians, means that the papers are relevant to any psychoanalytic psychotherapist in either child or adult practice. They also invite a welcome look at culture, society and politics within a psychoanalytic framework.

The book enables the reader to enter a lively discussion led by the topics of violence and aggression that develop through to theories on terrorism, fundamentalism, early infant deprivation and the effects of abuse in its many forms.

The Ghost in the Machine: IAPT and Organizational Melancholia

Rosemary Rizq

Rosemary Rizq

Roehampton University, Holybourne Avenue, London SW15 4JD. [r.rizq@roehampton.ac.uk]

Rosemary Rizq  

IAPT, melancholia, organizational dynamics, primary care

The introduction, funding and roll-out of the NHS's Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) programme represents one of the biggest changes to mental health service provision ever seen in the UK. Drawing on Hinshelwood's (1994) notion that public mental health services may be regarded as a defence against overwhelming anxieties relating to psychological fragility and emotional distress, I explore the tendency for IAPT services to systematically disavow feelings of loss and vulnerability in both staff and patients. I propose three mechanisms by which this disavowal occurs: the promotion of a consumerist ethos and a ‘patient choice’ agenda; the deployment of discourses minimizing notions of fragility and dependence; and the proliferation of bureaucratic and surveillance systems aimed at continually monitoring and evaluating staff and clinical activity. Drawing on Freud's (1917) distinction between mourning and melancholia, I go on to argue that a sense of unconscious loss may come to be constitutive of the culture within IAPT services where the institutionally-sanctioned repudiation of containment cannot be spoken about, addressed or mourned. Through a short case example, I illustrate the way in which organizational melancholia may be hidden within the structures of an IAPT service and enacted by both staff and patients.

Private Bag 3, Wits, 2050, South Africa. [Yael.Kadish@wits.ac.za]

anorexia, anti-analytic third, binge eating, countertransference, culture, eating disorder, feminist

A comprehensive understanding of eating disorders should include engagement with the role of contemporary cultural trends. Feminists and critical social theorists have made significant contributions in this regard. Using two clinical cases, this paper contemplates the relationship between culture and psyche in eating disorder, proposing a psychoanalytic conceptualization underpinned by John Steiner's (1982, 1987, 1993, 2011) theory of pathological organizations and psychic retreats. Two conceptual terms will be introduced, namely ‘the normalized body order’ and ‘the abject body object’ to develop the argument. One of the clinical cases will be used to explore a particular kind of therapeutic impasse that can occur when therapist and patient are both female. In this particular case, the normalized body order emerged temporarily obstructing therapeutic progress; the impasse was understood to be an example of the so-called anti-analytic third (Straker, 2006).

Salwa Jayyusi

Foundation for Psychotherapy and Counselling, London [salwaj@aol.com]

Salwa Jayyusi  

Dear Editor

Reading Martin Kemp's article forced me to reflect as to what degree, I, as a Palestinian living in Europe, had normalized and learned to accept the West's long-standing double standards with regards to Zionism, Israel, and the ongoing dispossession and oppression of the Palestinians. I am grateful to Dr Kemp for his article and to the BJP for publishing it.

The article did not, however, draw attention to the transgenerational impact of the ‘Nakba’ or ‘Catastrophe’ on the Palestinians. I am a child of parents who were amongst the 700,000 Palestinians who had to flee their towns and villages, mostly as a result of - what is now generally accepted as - ethnic cleansing by Zionist forces, in 1948. My father was born in Jerusalem and my mother in Haifa. They lived in Jerusalem until both had to leave, taking with them documents of ownership of their land in the belief that they would at some point be able to return home.

Although my parents did not have to endure living in refugee camps, they struggled to build a new life from scratch in another country that was hostile to them (as some Arab countries were). My father had to support 13 members of his family, which included his sister and her six children, whose father was murdered in Jerusalem by a Zionist while tending his shop.

Along with their ancestral homeland my parents' generation had lost a significant part of themselves leading to a confused and tortured sense of identity. Although I was born post-1948, I was deeply affected by their trauma and suffering. My children, third generation exiles, have not escaped that loss or confusion either, notwithstanding the privileges they may have enjoyed living and growing up in the West.

The trauma suffered by the Jews has been acknowledged by the world. Their experiences inform film, literature, journalism and the wider media. In contrast, Palestinian suffering has, until quite recently, been largely ignored. The dehumanization of the Palestinians, in Israel, the West Bank and Gaza continues with near total impunity (and we normalize the situation, perhaps because it poisons the soul always to be thinking). So the experience of trauma and loss is compounded and leaves no space for the healing process to begin. While this indifference is sadly the case in many parts of the world where oppression and injustice prevails, as Kemp suggests, the lack of objectivity regarding the Palestinian experience is surely exceptional. Whilst most serious and reputable historians do not dispute the historicity of the tragedy that befell and continues to befall the Palestinians, there is still need to effect such transparency and objectivity in other disciplines and professions.

Nick Duffell

Nick Duffell

[genderpsychology@btinternet.comwww.boardingschoolsurvivors.co.uk]

Nick Duffell  

Dear Editor

I applaud much of Elizabeth Standish's review (BJP 27(4): 417-19), but since she mentions me frequently I appreciate the chance to clarify my position. Her account of ex-boarders in her practice supports my observation made in April's Therapy Today (Duffell, 2011), that therapists and patients generally belong to the same social class that may normalize boarding. But with ‘It is easy to fall into a sense of blaming the therapists who did not draw out the trauma of early boarding’, she minimizes the issue. I cannot support this stance.

Since I began my work with ex-boarders in 1989 I have received thousands of letters from members of the public, responding to newspaper articles and eventually my book, The Making of Them (Duffell, 2000). Many correspondents told me their therapist missed boarding issues. By this I do not mean the trauma of what happened at school, regularly trivialized in our media, but how the experience of 24/7 boarding affects the adults these children become.

Standish recalls advice from her training: ‘If you go after the badger he's likely to retreat even further. But what if the badger never emerges?’ Badgers tend not to emerge because they are afraid. Ex-boarders are too - even if they don't show it. If they present for therapy, like all patients, they present symptoms rather than causes; it's our job to help them see the links. Additionally, boarding-school survivors harbour vicious internal double-binds from the shame of their privilege, so they tend not to come out from hiding - unless they find themselves in real crisis or in really safe hands.

Standish ends: ‘The world we live in is changing, British society is less repressive than it was - and we have mobile phones’. I find this argument naïve and dangerous. It is one frequently used by the Boarding Schools Association, with whom I have had much media debate. Boarders grow up without families, phones or not. Go to any boarding school and you'll rarely see unhappy children. Colin Luke's (1994) masterly film manages to catch some 8 year-olds in their first weeks. But later on all has been repressed: smiling faces are in place, mostly for life. It's the adult survivor, whose child has been sacrificed on the alter of privilege, who needs our help, but whose functional self will resist any attempt of deconstruction, as Standish's clinical vignette aptly demonstrates.

Attention to Culture and Diversity in Psychoanalytic Trainings

Karen Ciclitira and Nena Foster

Nena Foster

[k.ciclitira@mdx.ac.uk]

[nena@uel.ac.uk]

Nena Foster  

psychoanalytic training, culture, diversity, ethnicity, homosexuality, minority

Ethnically and culturally diverse groups increasingly undertake psychotherapy, but insufficient attention is often paid to aspects of diversity. This article explores qualitative data from a mixed-method study, conducted at a UK psychoanalytic psychotherapy training institution, in which 24 participants from diverse backgrounds were interviewed individually about their experiences of clinical training. Participants were asked how their ethnicity had impacted on their training, and also how social class, sexual orientation, religion and gender might affect the training experience. The data were analysed thematically, and a principal theme that emerged was the way that psychoanalytical clinical trainings tend, for theoretical reasons, to explore ‘internal’ psychological issues at the expense of ‘external’ material issues such as ethnicity. Similar concerns arose in connection with social class, gender and sexual orientation, with a specific theme being that of trainees feeling silenced and finding it difficult to openly discuss various aspects of diversity.

Maggie Turp PHD

Maggie Turp

73 Torbay Road, London NW6 7DU. [maggieturp@googlemail.com]

Maggie Turp  

adhesive identification, countertransference, psychic skin, psychotherapy, psychoanalysis, integrity, hard to reach patients

Certain states of mind in a patient are difficult to remain with and tend to evoke defensive countertransference responses which, if enacted, obstruct therapeutic progress. The state of mind discussed in this paper is ‘adhesive identification’, a term that arose out of a conversation between Esther Bick and Donald Meltzer, when Bick said of certain patients: ‘They are sticky, they stick …’ The author presents an outline of ‘psychic skin’ defences (Bick, 1968, 1986; Briggs, A., 2002; Briggs, S., 1998; Mitrani, 2001; Turp, 2003) followed by a more detailed account of ‘adhesive identification’ (Meltzer, 1975). Cohen's (2003) work on countertransference and integrity, based on her experiences in a neonatal intensive care unit, is described. These resources are employed as a framework for thinking about countertransference enactments arising in psychoanalytic psychotherapy with an adult, adhesively attached patient. Extracts from a session with the patient, ‘Janine’, are presented and discussed. In conclusion, the author returns to the proposed links between integrity in the sense of thoughtfulness and respect and integrity in the sense of the felt experience of being in one piece within a skin boundary.
